paragraphs: The following judgments concern how logisticians work in practice. They do not predict hiring, qualifications, authorization, or contract outcomes.

Logisticians turn organizational logistics needs into deliverable supply solutions: maintaining client relationships and fulfilling requirements, managing subcontractors and logistics performance, directing the availability and allocation of materials and finished products, redesigning goods flows to optimize value and costs, explaining solutions through proposals and presentations, guiding teams and reporting project progress, collaborating across departments, and keeping up with logistics technology.

Entirely fictional logistics solution sample: provide a fictional supply scenario containing 1 materials and inventory summary, 1 transportation route needing optimization, 1 subcontractor delay, and 1 cost constraint. Within 60 minutes, write requirements analysis, solution comparisons, subcontracting and risk handling, and key points for management reporting. Do not use real company, supplier, or contract data.

Sample output and reflection: check whether requirements and constraints were verified first, solutions were compared on comparable terms, and assumptions and risk explanations were retained. Then ask yourself whether you can stay organized under multi-party coordination and time pressure, support judgments with data, and accept responsibility for solutions and outcomes.

Logisticians on this page refers to O*NET 13-1081.00: analyzing and coordinating the ongoing logistical functions of a firm or organization, covering logistics throughout the product life cycle, including acquisition, distribution, internal allocation, delivery, and final disposal of resources; maintaining client relationships, managing subcontractors and logistics performance, directing material and finished-product allocation, optimizing goods flows, and supporting decisions through proposals and reports. Work mainly involves offices and cross-department coordination, with data analysis, project coordination, and supply-chain risks. This page excludes adjacent roles such as industrial production managers, production planning and expediting clerks, purchasing managers, and supply chain managers.

entries: Work inputs: client requirements and service levels, inventory and materials data, transportation and warehousing resources, subcontractors and contracts, logistics cost and performance metrics, and project plans and progress.

Checkable outputs: requirements analyses and solution comparisons, subcontractor performance specifications and review records, goods-flow optimization recommendations and cost estimates, project progress and results reports, and reviewable logistics performance metrics.

Full workflow: understand client needs and service agreements → collect inventory, transportation, and cost data → design and compare logistics solutions → select and manage subcontractors → direct material and finished-product allocation → monitor performance and optimize goods flows → report project results.

paragraphs: Key judgments: how to quantify needs and service levels, which comparable definitions to use in solution comparisons, how to set subcontractor selection and performance standards, how to balance cost and timeliness, and which risks require escalation to management or contracting parties.

Environment and pace: mainly indoor office work with frequent use of computers, spreadsheets, and data systems and communication with clients, subcontractors, and internal departments. Project milestones and peak seasons create time pressure, requiring progress through multi-party coordination.

Research inputs: occupational identity, tasks, work activities, work context, interest codes, and tools and technology information from O*NET 13-1081.00. Findings apply to the exact US occupation and do not establish mainland Chinese qualifications, pay, or employment definitions.

Check first: client requirements and service-level agreements, inventory and transportation data definitions, cost and timeliness constraints, subcontracting agreements and performance standards, project milestones, and assumptions and risk explanations to retain.

Work cycle: start with understanding needs and agreements, proceed through data collection, solution design and comparison, subcontractor management, execution and monitoring, then optimize performance and report results. Do not proceed until data definitions and constraints are confirmed.

Boundaries with adjacent roles: this page covers logisticians only. Industrial production managers oversee production sites and capacity; production planning and expediting clerks execute planning and material follow-up; purchasing managers manage purchasing functions; supply chain managers oversee end-to-end supply-chain strategy. Authority and final responsibilities cannot be interchanged with this role.

Industrial production managers oversee production sites, capacity, and personnel, delivering production results. Logisticians coordinate logistics functions and goods-flow solutions, delivering executable supply and logistics solutions.

Production planning and expediting clerks follow up materials and delivery dates under plans, focusing on execution. Logisticians design solutions, manage subcontractors, and review performance, with broader decision-making and coordination scope.

Purchasing managers oversee purchasing functions and supplier strategy. Logisticians manage logistics functions spanning transportation, warehousing, distribution, and goods-flow optimization, with different responsibilities.

Supply chain managers oversee end-to-end supply-chain strategy and cross-functional governance. Logisticians focus on logistics solutions, execution coordination, and performance improvement, generally with narrower strategic and governance authority.
Boundaries of AI's impact on logisticians

Editorial trial candidate: use fictional requirements, inventory, cost, and transportation information to test aggregation, solution comparison, and performance reporting. Optimization algorithms, TMS, or forecasting software are not evidence of generative AI adoption rates. Authorized parties review assumptions, constraints, subcontracting agreements, and solution tradeoffs.

Occupational sources describe the tasks and objects actually handled in this occupation: client needs, inventory and transportation data, subcontractors and contracts, cost and performance metrics, and project coordination. Tool capabilities, organizational adoption, and job outcomes are recorded separately; wage or employment data do not substitute for AI evidence.

Editorial task breakdown: the assistance steps above are candidates for validation. This round obtained neither a ranking of automation difficulty across steps nor evidence of actual adoption outcomes. On-site judgment and authorized responsibilities require confirmation by the personnel responsible for the role.

Human control points are verifying data definitions and constraints, judging solution tradeoffs, managing subcontractors and handling exceptions, and taking responsibility for solution outcomes and performance records.

First conduct offline solution exercises using entirely fictional supply scenarios and data summaries, recording assumptions, comparisons, and escalation paths. Do not let unverified system forecasts replace judgment.
Editorial suggestion: tools may assist with route optimization, demand forecasting, and performance tracking. Current materials do not demonstrate widespread adoption of these systems by companies.
Base decisions on data definitions and contractual constraints, retaining human judgment and records.

This round did not establish a separate Chinese wage mapping for Logisticians. NBS2025 transportation, storage, and postal services figures of 133981 / 73133 yuan are only broad industry proxies for such businesses. They do not cover all manufacturing, government, or other employers and are not occupational medians or starting pay.

Statistical scope: the National Bureau of Statistics 2025 average annual wage for employed persons in transportation, storage, and postal services was {{fact:cn-transport-nonprivate-wage}} for urban non-private units and {{fact:cn-transport-private-wage}} for urban private units. The nationwide total for urban non-private units was {{fact:cn-national-nonprivate-wage}}. All are industry-level statistics, not this occupation's median or starting pay.

Category boundary: the Ministry of Human Resources and Social Security publishes enterprise compensation survey information by occupation / position, which can be used to look up related logistics and supply-chain pay. This page did not obtain an entry matching O*NET 13-1081.00 exactly and does not treat it as this occupation's national median. Refer to competent authorities' publications for specifics.

Insufficient evidence: no nationwide occupational median wage, statistical period, or definition corresponding to logisticians in mainland China was obtained. This page shows only an industry proxy labeled as industry-level data; it does not fill the gap with proxy figures or US figures.
US logistician pay and employment statistics

The table below shows US nationwide 2025 OEWS wage percentiles. Median wages and hourly values are used separately as reported by the occupational source. Separate employment projections are 255,100 workers in 2025 and 300,000 in 2035, 18% growth over 2025—2035, and 26,600 average annual openings from growth and replacement.

2025 nationwide occupational wage percentiles are not starting pay or take-home income. This round did not verify whether performance bonuses are widespread across the occupation; verify payment components for each contract.

The 10th and 90th percentiles mark boundaries within this occupation's nationwide US wage distribution, not entry-level or senior grades. The percentile table cannot separate the effects of education, experience, location, employer, or other factors.

O*NET2025 employment industries: manufacturing 22%, government 15%, professional, scientific, and technical services 15%, management of companies 11%, transportation and warehousing 11%, and wholesale trade 11%. US shares are not Chinese industry distributions, wages, or hiring-demand projections.

Employment in 2025: 255,100; growth over 2025—2035: 18%. Average annual openings of 26,600 include replacements and are neither currently advertised positions nor annual net additions. They do not establish individual opportunity or AI causation.
Fit signals: start with observable work behavior

To assess fit, first consider whether you can remain organized under multi-party coordination and time pressure, support solution tradeoffs with data and comparable definitions, manage subcontractors and exceptions, and accept responsibility for solution outcomes. Tools such as RIASEC can only suggest hypotheses; they cannot replace real task experience.

Positive signals: attention to detail and ability to organize complex data, willingness to communicate with clients and across departments, measuring performance against goals and standards, and staying organized under pressure while recording assumptions truthfully.

Conditions for caution: unwillingness to handle large amounts of data and spreadsheets, losing focus during multi-party coordination, difficulty making cost-versus-timeliness tradeoffs, or unwillingness to take responsibility for solutions.
Trial action: use an entirely fictional supply scenario and data summary to practice requirements analysis, solution comparison, and risk explanations. Ask another person to review the records.

The RIASEC interest code is CEI (Conventional—Enterprising—Investigative): a preference for processing data under procedures, advancing solutions in business settings, and analyzing problems. These labels describe activity preferences only; they cannot determine competence, qualifications, or authorization.

This round obtained no personality predictive-validity studies for logisticians. Compare solutions using fictional requirements, costs, and contractual constraints to observe data verification and coordination records. Do not use scales to judge hiring or budget authority.
Type tools such as MBTI and the Enneagram cannot determine competence or qualifications; they may only support self-reflection.

Entry paths and capability stages

O*NET75% of respondents consider a bachelor's degree necessary for new entrants, 8% high school or equivalent, and 8% a postsecondary certificate. These are not current workers' educational attainment shares. JobZone4 is a preparation grouping; verify employers' actual course, experience, and training requirements separately.

China has a national occupational skills standard for logistics service specialists (2020, 4-02-06-03), but it does not automatically equate to O*NET13-1081.00 or impose mandatory entry requirements for all positions. Verify target duties, assessment requirements, and employer authority separately in both countries. Skills assessments or training do not grant budget, contract-signing, or supplier-selection authority.

Training certificates, industry credentials, and position approval authority are different statuses. A credential does not automatically grant contract-signing, budget, or supplier-selection authority. Decisions outside the position's scope and authorization should be referred to authorized personnel.
Entry stage: practice organizing requirements, verifying data, and comparing solutions under supervision, participate in subcontractor and performance follow-up, and retain process records.
Evidence to demonstrate: use a reviewable requirements and solution comparison explanation, cost estimates, and performance metric records to demonstrate data-driven judgment.
Next step: verify the target employer's duties, system and data access, and supplier management boundaries, then validate solution design and coordination skills in supervised real projects.

Moving toward greater responsibility: with experience, take responsibility for more complex networks or projects, instruct new workers, or move into supply-chain, purchasing, and operations management.
Market signals and transition directions

US O*NET / BLS: employment of 255,100 in 2025, projected 300,000 in 2035, 18% growth over 2025—2035, and 26,600 average annual openings from growth and replacement. Occupational projections are neither current hiring samples nor individual hiring probabilities.

O*NET2025 employment industries: manufacturing 22%, government 15%, professional, scientific, and technical services 15%, management of companies 11%, transportation and warehousing 11%, and wholesale trade 11%. US shares are not Chinese industry distributions, wages, or hiring-demand projections.

Transferable capabilities: requirements analysis and data organization, solution design and cost estimates, subcontractor and contract management, performance metrics and project coordination, and cross-department communication.

Transitioning to industrial production management requires production-site, capacity-scheduling, quality and equipment-safety management skills and evidence of personnel appointment. Logistics goods-flow solutions do not automatically cover manufacturing management responsibilities.

source_card.note: 13-1081.00 Logisticians covers full-life-cycle logistics analysis and coordination, not just 13-1081.02 Logistics Analysts. Current 2025 wages: 50890 / 64440 / 82320 / 106190 / 133160, hourly 39.58; 2025—2035 employment 255100 → 300000, 18%, openings 26600. 2025 industry shares: manufacturing 22 / government 15 / professional services 15 / management of companies 11 / transportation 11 / wholesale 11%. CEI describes activity preferences; education surveys new entrants' requirements. NBS2025 transportation figures are proxies only. China's 2020 logistics service specialist standard does not equal mandatory entry or the US code. Protected identity / CTA, FAQ, and shared sources retain older titles, projections, education, and qualification statements pending review. Exact Chinese wages, AI and personality evidence, and detailed-industry wages remain gaps.

description.text: Logisticians on this page refers to O*NET 13-1081.00: analyzing and coordinating organizational logistics functions covering acquisition, distribution, internal allocation, delivery, and resource disposal; managing subcontractors and logistics performance, optimizing goods flows, and guiding teams. Work mainly involves offices and cross-department coordination. When assessing this career path, verify the full work cycle, responsibility boundaries, evidence scope, risk controls, and observable entry-level work samples together.

title.text: Logistician Career Assessment: Work, Entry Paths, and Risk Boundaries

subject.name: Logistics Analyst
subject.summary: Logisticians on this page refers to O*NET 13-1081.00: analyzing and coordinating a firm's or organization's ongoing logistics functions throughout the product life cycle, including acquisition, distribution, internal allocation, delivery, and final resource disposal; maintaining client relationships and fulfilling needs; managing subcontractors by reviewing proposals, developing performance specifications, and serving as liaison; reviewing logistics performance against goals and service levels; directing availability and allocation of materials and finished products; and redesigning goods flows to maximize value and minimize costs. They explain solutions to clients and management through written proposals and presentations, guide teams and report project progress, collaborate across departments, and follow logistics technology improvements. Work mainly involves offices and cross-department coordination, with data analysis, project coordination, and supply-chain risks. This page excludes adjacent roles such as industrial production managers, production planning and expediting clerks, purchasing managers, and supply chain managers.
